# Model Tree

A schema describes what belongs together. Leaves represent typed values;
branches combine related values into context; the root represents one
observation. The same tree defines where reconstruction targets and exported
embeddings live.

## Follow One Observation

An order can contain several line items. This is one illustrative record:

```yaml
customer_tier: gold
line_items:
  - sku: A12
    quantity: 2
    price: 19.99
  - sku: B07
    quantity: 1
    price: 45.50
returned: false
```

The parent supplies each child's name:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model(
    d_model=64,
    n_layers=2,
    n_heads=4,
    customer_tier=rf.Category,
    line_items=rf.Branch(
        length=32,
        sku=rf.Category,
        quantity=rf.Number,
        price=rf.Number,
    ),
    returned=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

```{typst}
//| label: fig-model-tree
//| fig-alt: An order combines customer tier and repeated line items containing SKU, quantity, and price, and predicts whether it was returned.
//| fig-cap: Line-item context reaches the order context. The return target supplies no encoder input.
#tree(node("order", kind: "root", children: (
  node("customer_tier", type: "Category"),
  node("line_items", kind: "branch", repeated: true, children: (
    node("sku", type: "Category"),
    node("quantity", type: "Number"),
    node("price", type: "Number"),
  )),
  node("returned", kind: "target", type: "Boolean"),
)))
```

Fields at the same line-item position belong to the same item. The branch
contextualizes those inputs and reduces the item collection before routing it
to the order. The root combines that representation with customer tier.
`mask=True` keeps the return answer out of the encoder and creates its
reconstruction objective.

A decoder pools representations along its ancestor path. Learned decoder
queries can also be conditioned on visible sibling representations when their
coordinates align. It is therefore misleading to treat every decoder as
reading only the root, or to treat a tree edge as a database join. Explicit
joins and derived values belong in [preprocessing](../guides/preprocessors.qmd).

## Names And Addresses

The generated root is anonymous and has address `/`. It is always a singleton;
repeated data belongs in a child branch. There is no root-name option.
Diagrams use a descriptive root label such as `order` or `customer` to identify
the observation. That label is illustrative, not model configuration or an
address prefix; the root address remains `rf.Address()`.

A child branch reads a list even when `length=1`; a bare child mapping is not
a branch collection. Branch and leaf definitions have no `name` or positional
arguments.

Bare tensorfield classes such as `amount=rf.Number` and `sku=rf.Category` use
the field's defaults. Call them only to configure options, such as
`returned=rf.Boolean(mask=True)`. Reusing a definition creates independent
named nodes and learned modules; it does not share model weights.

Use a `fields` mapping when generating children or when a child name collides
with a configuration option:

```python
measurements = rf.Branch(
    length=8,
    fields={"length": rf.Number, "description": rf.Category},
)
```

An address starts with `/` and identifies a schema location, such as
`/line_items/price`. A field named `name` is an ordinary child: `name=rf.Category`
has address `/name`. The leading slash is not an input-data wrapper or a query.
Addresses appear in prediction fields, metric names, and mutation predicates.
They describe the model's structure even when an explicit `query` reads a
differently named source path. Names and nesting match input data by default;
see [Binding Data](binding-data.qmd) for other source layouts.

Use `rf.Address(...)` with one argument per child name to distinguish a schema
address from an ordinary data key or query string. The leading slash and
separators are added automatically; no arguments selects the root:

```python
root = rf.Address()
price = rf.Address("line_items", "price")
selected = model.select(rf.where("address") == price)
```

For example, `rf.Address("transactions", "amount")` represents
`/transactions/amount`. Serialized paths such as `/transactions/amount` can
also be read back with `rf.Address(path)`.

`rf.Address` is a string subclass, so the same value works with RelFlow
accessors and Arrow or Polars prediction-field lookups. Serialized output
still uses plain string keys.

## Configure The Context

`d_model`, `n_layers`, and `n_heads` are required when building with
`rf.Model(...)` from fields. The [size factories](#choose-a-size) supply defaults
for those settings and the rest of the tree. `d_model` is the shared embedding
width. The model's encoder settings configure the root; child branches have
their own settings.

| Setting | Controls |
| --- | --- |
| `attention` | The branch encoder: `"mha"`, `"gqa"`, `"mqa"`, or `None`. |
| `n_layers`, `n_heads`, `dropout` | That branch's encoder. |
| `reduction` | What the branch passes to its parent. Defaults to `rf.Attention()`. |
| `length` | Maximum retained records in a child branch. |
| `overflow` | Keep the first records (`"head"`, default), last records (`"tail"`), or raise (`"error"`). |
| `mask` | Which inputs to hide or reconstruct. |
| `embed=True` | Export the representation at that address. |

Encoder and reduction settings are separate. `attention=None` disables
encoder attention but leaves the selected reduction in place. An attention
reduction owns its `n_outputs`, `n_layers`, optional `n_heads`/`dropout`, and
`position`; omitted reduction heads/dropout inherit the branch values.
`rf.Mean()` averages present inputs. `reduction=None` preserves routed child
slots instead of summarizing them. See [Branch](../data-types/branch.qmd) for
the complete reduction contract.

Short collections are padded. Padding and structurally skipped inputs do not
contribute to attention or mean pooling. An explicit null remains a modeled
value state and is different from padding.

Only declared options are accepted. Use `description` for notes. A leaf's
`active=False` excludes it from execution while retaining it in the schema;
change an existing model through [mutation methods](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd).
For learning and output roles, continue to [Masking](dynamic-masking.qmd) and
[Embeddings](embeddings.qmd).

## Choose A Size

`rf.Model.xs(...)`, `.sm(...)`, `.md(...)`, `.lg(...)`, and `.xl(...)` build the
same kinds of model trees with different capacity defaults. Start with `md`
for a nested relational task or `sm` for faster iteration, then compare on
validation data. These are starting configurations; schema size, vocabularies,
and decoded fields also affect parameter counts and compute.

The bundled revision-1 configurations are:

| Factory | Width | Root layers | Child branch layers | Heads | Root outputs | Child branch outputs |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| `rf.Model.xs` | 64 | 1 | 1 | 2 | 1 | 1 |
| `rf.Model.sm` | 128 | 2 | 1 | 4 | 2 | 2 |
| `rf.Model.md` | 256 | 3 | 2 | 8 | 4 | 4 |
| `rf.Model.lg` | 384 | 4 | 2 | 8 | 8 | 4 |
| `rf.Model.xl` | 512 | 6 | 3 | 8 | 16 | 8 |

Every child branch receives its preset defaults at every depth. All five
presets use MHA encoders, zero dropout, and attention reductions with one layer
and positional information. Reduction heads and dropout inherit their owning
branch. Leaf decoders use query pooling, one cross-attention block, zero
dropout, and the preset head count; their automatic positional policy remains
`decoder_position=None`.

For example, this model uses the `md` defaults for customer history, with an
explicit root depth and a larger history reduction:

```python
import relflow as rf

model = rf.Model.md(
    n_layers=4,
    balance=rf.Number,
    customer_tier=rf.Category,
    transactions=rf.Branch(
        length=128,
        overflow="tail",
        reduction=rf.Attention(n_outputs=8),
        merchant=rf.Category,
        amount=rf.Number,
        days_ago=rf.Number,
    ),
    returned=rf.Boolean(mask=True),
)
```

Explicit settings win at their own node. Here, `n_layers=4` configures only
the root; the transaction branch keeps two encoder layers. A leaf's decoder
heads remain independent of its parent's overrides. Changing `d_model` changes
the shared width and must remain compatible with every effective head count.

An explicit reduction replaces the whole preset reduction. Passing
`reduction=rf.Attention()` selects its one-output defaults even under `xl`.
`rf.Mean()` and `None` also retain their usual behavior. Explicit values equal
to ordinary defaults still win, including `n_layers=1` on a branch and
`dropout=None` for zero dropout. Reusing a branch or field definition across
different factories leaves that definition unchanged.

Presets leave collection lengths, overflow, queries, masking, datatype options,
optimizer settings, and runtime settings under application control. They keep
the anonymous singleton root at `/`. Reduction outputs are context vectors;
they do not create prediction records. With `embed=True`, `xs` exports one
width-64 root vector, while `md` exports four width-256 root vectors. Set
`reduction=rf.Attention(n_outputs=1)` explicitly when an application needs one
root vector, and evaluate that bottleneck.

The resolved schema records the actual architecture. `model.preset` holds the
selected immutable policy, including its name and revision; ordinary
`rf.Model(...)` construction has no preset policy. Restore a schema directly
with `rf.Model(schema=schema)`; preset factories reject `schema=...`.

The factories bind immutable configurations from `rf.presets`. An application
can use the same factory to declare a classmethod on its own subclass:

```python
import relflow as rf

class SupportModel(rf.Model):
    compact = rf.presets.factory(rf.presets.SM)
```

`SupportModel.compact(...)` accepts the usual model construction keywords and
returns a `SupportModel` with the bound `sm` defaults.

Checkpoints retain the full original preset policy alongside the resolved
schema. New nodes added with [`extend(...)`](../guides/schema-mutation.qmd)
receive those saved defaults after loading, even if the bundled configurations
change later. Existing nodes keep their resolved settings. A schema-only model
constructed without a saved policy uses ordinary defaults when extending it.
